analysis.one_liner: Forces the federal government to start taking nuclear plant waste to a Nevada storage site by 2003, bypassing normal environmental review.
analysis.headline: The bill had 136 cosponsors and cleared a House committee 40-6, but it was never brought to the House floor and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill rewrites the 1982 nuclear waste law to order the Energy Department to begin accepting spent fuel from civilian nuclear plants by June 30, 2003, store it temporarily at the Nevada Test Site, and eventually bury it at Yucca Mountain. It locks in a 1-mill-per-kilowatt-hour fee on nuclear generation paid by electric customers, and lets utilities pay a one-time fee that wipes out all of their future waste-disposal obligations. To hit the deadline, it skips environmental review for key siting and construction decisions, replaces the EPA's independent radiation standard with its own, and blocks courts from stopping construction while licensing is pending.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners of civilian nuclear power reactors gain the most: the bill orders the federal government to take their waste by a fixed 2003 deadline, lets them keep waste on site at government expense and title, and lets a one-time fee extinguish every future storage and disposal obligation. Host counties in Nevada (Nye, Lincoln, and the City of Caliente) gain payments and federal land. Emergency responders and transport workers gain funded training programs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Nuclear utilities and Nevada host counties

how_it_helps.text: Orders the Energy Department to be able to accept and transport spent nuclear fuel and high-level waste by June 30, 2003, ending years of missed deadlines to nuclear plant operators.
Sets routes that minimize shipments through populated areas and, to the extent practicable, avoids routing waste through the Las Vegas metropolitan area.
Provides technical assistance and money for training public safety officials, emergency responders, and workers who handle the waste, funded from the Nuclear Waste Fund.
Gives Nevada host counties benefit agreements ($2.5 million a year and $5 million on first waste receipt), land conveyances, and payments in lieu of taxes.
Lets the Secretary take title to spent fuel and store it on reactor sites to relieve utilities of the financial burden of on-site storage.

analysis.who_pays: Electricity customers pay the 1-mill-per-kilowatt-hour fee on nuclear generation that funds the program. Nevada residents along the transport routes bear the shipments, with limited ability to sue or block construction, and the public loses environmental review of the storage site decisions, the EPA's independent radiation release standard, and the ability to hold the government liable for missed deadlines.
analysis.who_pays_short: Ratepayers, Nevada communities, and environmental oversight

drawbacks.text: The bill says designating the interim storage site, filing the license application, and constructing and operating the facility do not require an environmental impact statement or any environmental review, and the required environmental impact statement cannot consider the need for the facility, alternative sites, or alternative designs.

It strips the EPA of authority to set radiation release standards for the repository and substitutes a 100-millirem annual dose standard evaluated over 10,000 years, with compliance after the first 1,000 years judged only as 'likely' under a model.

No court may enjoin construction or operation of the interim storage facility before its final review of the licensing decision, and federal courts of appeals get original and exclusive jurisdiction over civil actions under the act.

Paying the one-time fee relieves the waste's owner of any further financial obligation to the federal government for long-term storage and permanent disposal, capping the industry's liability for waste that must be isolated for millennia.

The United States bears no financial liability for the Secretary's failure to meet any deadline in the act, and contract amendments waive contract holders' right to sue over missed acceptance deadlines going forward.
Accepting benefits does not count as Nevada's consent, but the state has no veto over the siting; the bill gives the Atomic Energy Act preeminence in any conflict with other law.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The federal government did owe utilities a disposal program that ratepayers had been funding since 1982, and moving decades of waste off scattered reactor sites has real safety logic, especially with funded training for responders and routes designed to avoid cities. But the bill pursues that goal by waiving environmental review of the siting decisions themselves, overruling the EPA's independent radiation standard, restricting court access, and permanently capping the generators' liability. The savings in oversight are the point of the deadline, and the costs fall on Nevada's communities, on ratepayers through the fee, and on future generations whose protections are written down by this statute.

outcome.mechanism: It cleared committee by 40-6 and was placed on the House calendar in June 1999, but no floor vote was ever scheduled before the Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Fred Upton introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, with 46 original cosponsors, and it drew 136 cosponsors in total, 88 Republicans and 48 Democrats.
The Commerce subcommittee forwarded it unanimously, 25-0, on April 14, 1999, and the full committee ordered it reported, 40-6, on April 21, 1999.

The committee reported it amended on May 20, 1999; the Resources and Budget committees were discharged from further consideration on June 2, 1999, and it was placed on the Union Calendar, Calendar No. 92.
The bill's action history shows no House floor vote or further action after June 2, 1999, through the end of the 106th Congress on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Nuclear utilities kept the status quo, still storing waste on site and pressing their claims over missed federal deadlines, while Nevada avoided a statutorily mandated interim storage facility built with weakened environmental review.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Utilities kept the status quo; Nevada avoided the facility

for.name: Fred Upton
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on January 6, 1999, and shepherded it through the Energy and Commerce Committee.

for.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
for.what_they_did: Voted 25-0 in subcommittee and 40-6 in full committee to report the bill amended on May 20, 1999.

against.name: House Republican leadership
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the House floor after it was placed on the calendar in June 1999; no vote occurred before the Congress ended.

against.name: State of Nevada
against.role: Host state for the proposed interim storage site and repository
against.what_they_did: Opposed the siting of nuclear waste storage and waste shipments in Nevada; the bill itself includes provisions barring legal arguments that accepting benefits constituted Nevada's consent.

sides.party_line_note: Support was bipartisan: 136 cosponsors split 88 Republicans and 48 Democrats, and the committee reported the bill 40-6 with no party breakdown of the six no votes recorded in the action history.

industries.note: The bill locks in their arrangement: customers pay a 1-mill-per-kilowatt-hour fee into the Nuclear Waste Fund, and the industry gets a guaranteed federal pickup of its waste by 2003 plus a one-time fee that extinguishes all future disposal liability for waste requiring permanent isolation. Their gain comes at ratepayer and host-community expense.

industries.industry: State of Nevada and communities along waste transport routes
industries.note: The bill mandates an interim storage facility at the Nevada Test Site with rail-to-truck transfer at Caliente and heavy-haul truck routes, while waiving environmental review of siting decisions and limiting courts' ability to stop construction. Host counties receive payments, but accepting them cannot be treated as consent and the state has no veto.

industries.industry: Nye and Lincoln counties and the City of Caliente
industries.note: They would receive benefit agreements ($2.5 million annually, $5 million on first waste receipt), land conveyances, and payments in lieu of taxes, plus funding for emergency-response training. The payments come in exchange for hosting a facility their state opposed.

The bill directs the Energy Department to use private industry 'to the fullest extent possible' for every aspect of transporting the waste, creating large contracts for rail and trucking carriers. They profit from moving hazardous material through populated corridors.
